periods.activity_title: Raghav's Yoga: Reading Clocks and Finding Duration

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q1–Q3, p.155
tasks_in_class.description: Read the two clock images showing Raghav's yoga start and end times; find how long he spent practising.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c), p.155
tasks_in_class.description: Find the time elapsed between given time periods (01:15 p.m. to 01:42 p.m.; 03:18 p.m. to 08:18 p.m.; 09:15 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.) and share strategies.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q6, p.156
tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats in a given table.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q7, p.156
tasks_in_class.description: Match each time in 12-hour format to its equivalent in 24-hour format.

homework.book_ref: Let us find out Q5 (a)(b), p.155
homework.description: Using the table of painting times (Raghav 1 hr 20 min, Rani 2 hr 10 min, Ritu 1 hr 35 min), identify who took longest and who took least time.

time_bands.activity: Children look at the two clock faces in Let us find out Q1–Q3 (p.155) ("Read Raghav's yoga start and end times....") and read the times aloud in pairs, then count forward in minutes to find how long he practised. Share two or three children's counting strategies with the class.

Children work on Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c) (p.155) ("Find elapsed time between given time periods....") individually, choosing their own strategy — counting on, subtracting, or using a number line drawn on their slate. Invite different strategies to the board; the class compares which feels easiest for each pair.

Introduce the 12-hour and 24-hour clock through a brief discussion of when each is used (transport timetables, daily life). Children fill in Let us find out Q6 (p.156) ("Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time....") using the pattern they notice in the table.

Children complete the matching activity in Let us find out Q7 (p.156) ("Match each time in 12-hour format to its 24-hour equivalent.") as a quick-fire pair game — one partner reads aloud, the other draws the matching line. Class confirms answers together.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating noon as 00:00 rather than 12:00 in 24-hour format; highlight this in the Q6 discussion. Where children struggle to find elapsed time, encourage them to count forward to the next whole hour first, then add the remaining minutes.
materials: Slates or paper for number lines

section_titles: Seconds as a unit of time
periods.activity_title: Racing Seconds: When Minutes Are Not Enough

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate whether each listed activity (blinking, counting 1–20, melting ice-cube, etc.) takes seconds or minutes; tick the appropriate cell.
List events (other than those in the table) that can happen in less than a minute or in a few seconds.
Time yourself: how many times can you skip rope in 10 seconds; how long to write FRIEND; how long to run 100 m.

homework.description: Estimate then verify how many balloons, push-ups, breaths, or hops you can do in one minute; record estimated and actual numbers.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the walking-race story (Akira, Sunita, Mary — each took 1 minute and a few seconds). Ask: 'Why can't we say all three finished at the same time?' Establish that 1 minute = 60 seconds and that seconds give the precision needed. Draw the stopwatch reading for each child on the board and identify the winner together.

Children complete Let Us Do (p.157) ("Estimate whether each activity takes seconds or minutes...."), ticking independently first. Pairs then compare and argue about any disagreements, building a shared class column on the board through a show-of-hands count.

Children add their own examples to Let Us Do (p.158) ("List events that can happen in less than a minute or a few seconds...."). Each child writes at least two personal examples; a quick round-the-class share collects surprising ones on the board.

Children carry out the timed tasks in Let Us Find Q1–Q3 (p.158) ("Time yourself: skip rope in 10 seconds; write FRIEND; run 100 m.") in rotation using the school clock or a count-aloud timer. Each child records their own results. Bring the class together to compare: who skipped most, who wrote fastest?

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is confusing the size of a second with a minute — children often say 'blinking takes a minute' before they have a felt sense of the second. The timed physical tasks provide the embodied correction; keep the count-aloud rhythm steady. For the 100 m run, use a wide corridor or the schoolyard and have pairs count aloud together.

section_titles: Reading seconds on a clock face
periods.activity_title: The Third Hand: Reading and Drawing Seconds

tasks_in_class.description: Observe four clock-pair images; read and fill in the number of seconds each child took (getting out of bed, moving to kitchen, picking up paper, washing plate).
Draw the missing seconds hand on the right-side clock for four given durations (20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 40 sec).

time_bands.activity: Display or draw a clock face on the board showing all three hands. Discuss: 'Which hand moves fastest? What does it count?' Establish that the seconds hand sweeps the full circle in 60 seconds, passing each number mark (where each number = 5 seconds). Count around the dial together as a class.

Children open to the clock-pair images in Let Us Do (p.159) ("Observe four clock-pair images; read the seconds each child took...."). For each pair, they identify the start position and end position of the seconds hand, count the arc, and write the elapsed seconds. Circulate and prompt: 'Where did the hand start? How many marks did it move?'

Children complete Let Us Do (p.160) ("Draw the missing seconds hand for four given durations...."). They decide where the hand must point for 20, 30, 60, and 40 seconds and draw it on the blank clock face. Pairs check each other's drawings; discuss: 'Where does the hand land after exactly 60 seconds and why?'

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating each number on the clock as one second rather than five seconds; the class count-around at the opening directly addresses this. For drawing the hand, encourage children to count by fives rather than trying to count sixty individual marks.
materials: Rulers or straight edges for drawing hands
Chalk clock on board or large clock diagram

section_titles: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
periods.activity_title: Double Number Lines: Hopping Between Hours, Minutes, Seconds

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the double number line by filling in missing hours and minutes values using the ×2 relationship shown.
Convert: 1 hr 10 min, 2 hr 45 min, 3 hr 15 min, 4 hr 20 min to minutes; and 75 min, 150 min, 220 min, 390 min to hours and minutes.
Fill the min↔sec double number line; convert 320 sec, 225 sec, 700 sec, 1000 sec to min and sec; convert 10 min 13 sec, 4 min 8 sec, 15 min 40 sec to seconds.

time_bands.activity: Draw a double number line on the board showing hours on top and minutes below. Fill in 0–1–2–3 hours and ask children to supply the minutes. Pose: '2 hours and 45 minutes — how many minutes altogether?' Let children suggest methods before reading the textbook dialogue. Establish 1 hr = 60 min as the multiplier.

Children complete Let Us Do Q1(a) (p.161) ("Complete the double number line filling in missing hours and minutes....") individually, then check with a partner. Class confirms the pattern: each step multiplies by 60. Transition to Q1(b)(i–viii) (p.161) ("Convert mixed hour-minute quantities to minutes and back.") — children work in pairs, sharing how they handle the leftover minutes.

Introduce the minutes-to-seconds double number line using the same structure. Ask: 'If 1 min = 60 sec, where does 3 min land?' Children draw their own number line on paper and fill it to 5 minutes. They then attempt Let Us Do Q1(c)(i–vii) (p.162) ("Fill the min↔sec number line; convert seconds to minutes and seconds and vice versa.") individually.

Quick class review: call out conversion problems orally (e.g. '225 seconds — how many minutes and seconds?') and take rapid answers. Address the most common sticking points from circulation. Children note any corrections on their paper.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is multiplying when dividing is needed (e.g. converting 75 minutes to hours by multiplying by 60 rather than dividing). Using the number line as a direction cue — moving left means dividing, right means multiplying — helps children self-correct. Children who have worked with the hours-and-minutes number line move more confidently to the minutes-and-seconds line.

section_titles: Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
periods.activity_title: Oral Strategies: Solving Time Word Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Raghav studies 4 subjects at 50 minutes each; find total time in hours and minutes and share strategies.
Raghu leaves at 08:00 hours and arrives at 09:05 hours; find time taken to reach Nana ji's house.

Solve word problems: find return/finish time given start time and duration, or find start time given finish time and duration (Jyoti, Ragini, picnic group, Raji, Alya, lunch break, 08:35 PM problems).

time_bands.activity: Present the worked example from the textbook: Raghu travels 08:00 to 09:05 — how long? Model the oral strategy aloud: count forward from 08:00 to 09:00 (that is 1 whole hour) then add 5 more minutes. Ask: 'Can someone explain this another way?' Take one or two alternative oral approaches from children.

Children solve Let Us Do Q2 (p.162) ("Raghav studies 4 subjects at 50 minutes each; find total time....") and Q3 (p.162) ("Raghu leaves at 08:00, arrives at 09:05; find time taken.") independently, writing their strategy in words alongside their answer. Pairs compare strategies; invite one pair per problem to share.

Children work through Let Us Do Q4–Q10 (p.163) ("Solve word problems finding return or start times given a duration....") in small groups of three. Each group assigns problems so every child solves at least two. Groups circulate answers for checking; flag disagreements for class discussion.

Whole-class closing discussion: choose one problem where a group disagreed (e.g. a problem that crosses noon). Ask: 'What made this trickier? How did you decide?' Reinforce the strategy of counting to the next whole hour first, then adding the remaining minutes.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is adding hours and minutes separately without regrouping — children write '1 hour 65 minutes' instead of converting the extra 5 minutes to give '2 hours 5 minutes'. Problems that cross noon or midnight (a.m. to p.m.) are a second sticking point; encourage children to count through 12 rather than subtract across it.

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Write two things you can do in less than one minute and two things that take more than one minute. For each, say whether seconds or minutes is the better unit to measure it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary. Examples for less than a minute (seconds): snapping fingers, clapping once. Examples for more than a minute (minutes): eating a meal, brushing teeth. The better unit is seconds for very quick actions and minutes for longer ones.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the size of the unit to the size of the duration — seconds for brief actions, minutes for longer ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: act out each event and count aloud to decide; stretch: estimate how many seconds each quick event takes.

exercise.description: List events (other than those in the table) that can happen in less than a minute or in a few seconds.

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Priya says she can write her name 3 times in 10 seconds. Arjun says he can write his name 5 times in 10 seconds. Without timing yourself, explain how you would check whose claim seems more believable.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A reasonable answer: count how many letters are in each name; a shorter name can be written more times in 10 seconds. Alternatively, try writing your own name once and estimate how many seconds it takes, then multiply. Arjun's claim is more believable if his name is short.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by counting the number of letters and comparing the time available.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them write their own name once while a partner counts slowly to 10; stretch: predict how many times they could write a longer or shorter word.

exercise.description: Time yourself: how many times can you skip rope in 10 seconds; how long to write FRIEND; how long to run 100 m.

items.section_title: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
items.prompt: A football match starts at 10:40 a.m. and ends at 12:25 p.m. How long did the match last? Show your steps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: From 10:40 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. is 20 minutes. From 11:00 a.m. to 12:25 p.m. is 1 hour 25 minutes. Total: 1 hour 45 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward to the next whole hour, then add the remaining time to the end time.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 10:40 to 12:25 and hop in whole-hour jumps; stretch: what time would the match end if it lasted 2 hours 10 minutes instead?

exercise.book_ref: Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c), p.155
exercise.description: Find the time elapsed between given time periods (01:15 p.m. to 01:42 p.m.; 03:18 p.m. to 08:18 p.m.; 09:15 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.) and share strategies.

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Which of these activities most likely takes only a few seconds?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sneezing once — it lasts only a second or two.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the size of each activity's duration to the size of a second (1/60 of a minute).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may not yet have a felt sense of how short a second is relative to a meal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is confusing a journey duration (many minutes) with a seconds-scale event.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has not yet anchored the second as a very small unit distinct from the many minutes needed to read.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: act out a sneeze and count — 'one'; then act out eating and count; feel the difference; stretch: rank all four activities from shortest to longest and give an estimate in seconds or minutes for each.

exercise.description: Estimate whether each listed activity (blinking, counting 1–20, melting ice-cube, etc.) takes seconds or minutes; tick the appropriate cell.

items.section_title: Reading seconds on a clock face
items.prompt: The seconds hand on a clock points to 12 at the start. After Meena finishes washing her hands, it points to 9. How many seconds did she take? Explain how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hand moved from 12 to 9, which is 45 seconds. Each number on the clock face represents 5 seconds, and from 12 to 9 going forward is 9 × 5 = 45 seconds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of clock-face numbers passed and multiply by 5 seconds each.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them count the number marks one by one on a drawn clock face; stretch: if she started at 3 instead of 12 and ended at 9, how many seconds would that be?

exercise.description: Observe four clock-pair images; read and fill in the number of seconds each child took (getting out of bed, moving to kitchen, picking up paper, washing plate).

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: Look at the double number line below. Which value belongs in the blank marked '?'
items.visual_stimulus:
number_line: 0 min | 60 min | 120 min | 180 min | ? min
number_line: 0 hr | 1 hr | 2 hr | 3 hr | 4 hr

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of hours by 60 to find the equivalent number of minutes.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may be adding 20 each time (noticing a different pattern) rather than using the ×60 relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be adding 40 each time, confusing the period duration with the conversion factor.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be adding 80 each time, possibly doubling the wrong value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: trace the number line step by step counting 60 each time; stretch: extend the number line to show 5 hours and 6 hours.

exercise.description: Complete the double number line by filling in missing hours and minutes values using the ×2 relationship shown.

items.section_title: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
items.prompt: A train departs at 14:30. What is this time in 12-hour format?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2:30 p.m. — subtract 12 from 14 to get 2, and hours after noon are p.m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 12 from the 24-hour value for any time from 13:00 onwards, and label it p.m.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child subtracted 12 correctly but confused a.m. and p.m. — does not yet link the 24-hour range 13–23 with afternoon.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have subtracted 10 instead of 12, confusing the conversion rule.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may believe 14:30 maps to 12:30 by removing only the tens digit, showing a procedural confusion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a side-by-side table showing 12:00–13:00–14:00 against noon–1 p.m.–2 p.m.; stretch: convert three more 24-hour times above 12:00 to 12-hour format.

exercise.book_ref: Let us find out Q6, p.156
exercise.description: Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats in a given table.

items.section_title: Reading seconds on a clock face
items.prompt: A clock's seconds hand points to 12. Draw where the seconds hand will point after exactly 30 seconds. Describe its position using a clock number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After 30 seconds the hand points to 6, because 30 ÷ 5 = 6 steps of 5 seconds each.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the number of seconds by 5 to find which clock-face number the hand reaches.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: count by fives on the clock face — 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 — and stop at 6; stretch: where would the hand be after 45 seconds?

exercise.description: Draw the missing seconds hand on the right-side clock for four given durations (20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 40 sec).

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: A cycling race lasted 2 hours and 35 minutes. How many minutes is that altogether?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply whole hours by 60, then add the remaining minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a number line marked in 60s — hop 60, then 60, then 35; stretch: convert the answer back to hours and minutes to check.

exercise.description: Convert: 1 hr 10 min, 2 hr 45 min, 3 hr 15 min, 4 hr 20 min to minutes; and 75 min, 150 min, 220 min, 390 min to hours and minutes.

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: A video clip is 245 seconds long. How many minutes and seconds is that?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 minutes and 5 seconds. 245 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 5. So 4 minutes and 5 seconds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total seconds by 60; the quotient is minutes and the remainder is seconds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: count up in 60s on a number line — 60, 120, 180, 240 — and see how many seconds are left over; stretch: convert 380 seconds to minutes and seconds.

exercise.description: Fill the min↔sec double number line; convert 320 sec, 225 sec, 700 sec, 1000 sec to min and sec; convert 10 min 13 sec, 4 min 8 sec, 15 min 40 sec to seconds.

items.section_title: Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
items.prompt: Kavya practises piano for 50 minutes each day for 5 days. What is the total practice time in hours and minutes?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 hours and 10 minutes. 50 × 5 = 250 minutes. 250 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 10. So 4 hours and 10 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply minutes per day by number of days, then divide by 60 to convert to hours and minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: add 50 five times on a number line and then convert to hours; stretch: if she adds a sixth day, what is the new total?

exercise.description: Raghav studies 4 subjects at 50 minutes each; find total time in hours and minutes and share strategies.

items.section_title: Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
items.prompt: A school function starts at 10:15 a.m. and ends after 2 hours and 40 minutes. At what time does it end?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12:55 p.m. From 10:15 a.m. add 2 hours to get 12:15 p.m., then add 40 minutes to get 12:55 p.m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add whole hours to the start time first, then add the remaining minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a time number line from 10:15, hop 2 hours to 12:15, then hop 40 minutes to 12:55; stretch: if the function ends at 1:10 p.m. instead, how long did it last?

exercise.description: Solve word problems: find return/finish time given start time and duration, or find start time given finish time and duration (Jyoti, Ragini, picnic group, Raji, Alya, lunch break, 08:35 PM problems).
